title: Chapter 13. Of the Natural Condition of Mankind, as Concerning Their Felicity, and Misery
paragraphs: Nature has made men so equal in the faculties of body and mind that, although one man may sometimes be clearly stronger in body or quicker of mind than another, when everything is reckoned together the difference between one man and another is not so considerable that one man can claim for himself any benefit to which another may not equally lay claim. As for bodily strength, the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, either by secret scheming or by joining with others who are in the same danger as himself.

And as for the faculties of the mind (setting aside the arts grounded on words, and especially that skill of proceeding by general and infallible rules called Science — which very few men have, and they only in a few things, as it is not an inborn faculty nor acquired, like Prudence, while we are looking after something else) — I find a still greater equality among men than there is in strength. For Prudence is just Experience, which equal time bestows equally on all men in those things to which they apply themselves equally. What may perhaps make such equality seem incredible is only a vain conceit of one's own wisdom, which almost every man thinks he has in a greater degree than the common sort — that is, than everyone but himself and a few others whom he approves, either because of their fame or because their opinions agree with his own. For such is the nature of men that, although they may acknowledge many others to be more clever, more eloquent, or more learned, they will hardly believe there are many as wise as themselves. They see their own wit at hand, and other men's at a distance. But this proves rather that men are equal in this point than unequal. For there is ordinarily no greater sign of the equal distribution of anything than that every man is contented with his share.

From this equality of ability arises equality of hope in attaining our ends. And therefore if any two men desire the same thing, which nevertheless they cannot both enjoy, they become enemies. And in pursuit of their end (which is principally their own preservation, and sometimes only their pleasure), they endeavor to destroy or subdue one another. From this it comes about that, where an invader has nothing more to fear than the single power of one other man, if one person plants, sows, builds, or settles on a convenient spot, others may probably be expected to come with their forces combined to dispossess him and to deprive him not only of the fruit of his labor but also of his life or liberty. And the invader, in turn, is in the like danger from another.

And given this mutual distrust, there is no way for any man to secure himself that is as reasonable as Anticipation — that is, by force or cunning to master the persons of all the men he can, until he sees no other power great enough to endanger him. This is no more than his own preservation requires, and is generally allowed. Also, since there are some who take pleasure in contemplating their own power in acts of conquest — pursuing it further than their security requires — if others, who would otherwise be glad to be at ease within modest bounds, were not by invasion to increase their power, they would not be able for long to subsist by standing only on the defensive. Consequently, such enlargement of dominion over other men, being necessary for a man's preservation, must be allowed him.

Again, men take no pleasure (but on the contrary a great deal of grief) in keeping company where there is no power able to overawe them all. For every man expects his companion to value him at the same rate he sets upon himself, and at any sign of contempt or undervaluing he naturally endeavors, so far as he dares (which, among those who have no common power to keep them in quiet, is far enough to make them destroy each other), to extort a greater valuation from those who scorn him — by damaging them, and from others by his example.
So in the nature of man we find three principal causes of quarrel. First, Competition; second, Diffidence; third, Glory.

The first makes men invade for gain; the second, for safety; and the third, for reputation. The first use violence to make themselves masters of other men's persons, wives, children, and cattle; the second, to defend them; the third, for trifles — a word, a smile, a different opinion, and any other sign of low estimation, whether directly aimed at their own persons or by reflection at their kindred, their friends, their nation, their profession, or their name.

From this it is plain that during the time men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition called War, and such a war as is of every man against every man (a war of all against all). For WAR consists not in battle only, or the act of fighting, but in a stretch of time in which the will to contend by battle is sufficiently known. And therefore the notion of Time is to be considered in the nature of war, as it is in the nature of weather. For just as the nature of foul weather lies not in a shower or two of rain but in an inclination toward it over many days together, so the nature of war consists not in actual fighting but in the known disposition to fight, during all the time there is no assurance to the contrary. All other time is PEACE.

Whatever therefore follows from a time of war, where every man is enemy to every man, the same follows from any time in which men live without any other security than what their own strength and their own invention will furnish them with. In such a condition there is no place for industry, because the fruit of it is uncertain — and consequently no cultivation of the earth; no navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by sea; no convenient building; no instruments for moving and removing such things as require much force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no account of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and, which is worst of all, continual fear and danger of violent death; and the life of man, “solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.”

It may seem strange to someone who has not weighed these things carefully that nature should thus pull men apart and make them apt to invade and destroy one another. He may therefore, not trusting this inference drawn from the passions, desire perhaps to have it confirmed by experience. Let him then consider with himself: when he takes a journey, he arms himself and seeks to travel well accompanied; when he goes to sleep, he locks his doors; even in his own house he locks his chests; and this when he knows there are laws and public officers, armed, to avenge any injury done to him. What opinion does he have of his fellow subjects when he rides armed? Of his fellow citizens when he locks his doors? And of his children and servants when he locks his chests? Does he not accuse mankind as much by his actions as I do by my words? But neither of us accuses man's nature in it. The desires and other passions of man are in themselves no sin. Nor are the actions that proceed from those passions, until they know a law that forbids them — which, until laws are made, they cannot know. Nor can any law be made until they have agreed on the person who shall make it.

It may perhaps be thought that there never was such a time, nor such a condition of war as this; and I believe it was never generally so over all the world. But there are many places where men live so now. For the savage people in many parts of America, except for the government of small families (whose concord depends on natural lust), have no government at all, and live to this day in that brutish manner I described before. In any case, what kind of life there would be where there was no common power to fear may be seen from the kind of life men who have formerly lived under a peaceful government degenerate into during a civil war.

But even if there had never been any time when individual men were in a condition of war against one another, in all times kings and persons of sovereign authority, because of their independence, are in continual jealousies, and in the state and posture of gladiators — their weapons pointing and their eyes fixed on one another. That is, their forts, garrisons, and guns are on the frontiers of their kingdoms, and they keep continual spies upon their neighbors, which is a posture of war. But because by these means they uphold the industry of their subjects, the misery that accompanies the liberty of private men does not follow from it.

From this war of every man against every man, this also follows: that nothing can be unjust. The notions of right and wrong, of justice and injustice, have no place there. Where there is no common power, there is no law; where there is no law, there is no injustice. Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues. Justice and injustice are not faculties of either the body or the mind. If they were, they might be in a man who was alone in the world, just as his senses and passions are. They are qualities that relate to men in society, not in solitude. It also follows from the same condition that there is no property, no dominion, no Mine and Thine distinct — only what each man can get, and for as long as he can keep it. And so much for the bad condition that man is actually placed in by mere nature, though with a possibility of coming out of it, lying partly in the passions and partly in his reason.

The passions that incline men to peace are: fear of death; desire of such things as are necessary for a comfortable life; and a hope of obtaining them by their industry. And reason suggests convenient articles of peace, on which men may be brought to agreement. These articles are what are otherwise called the Laws of Nature, of which I shall speak more particularly in the two following chapters.
